summary: The core is a gate-and-chip transcription of the Breakout TTL board. Every IC is its own module instance named by board position (DM9316_L1, SN7474_E6a, S82S16_L3), and every gate output is named by chip and gate letter (H2b, N4b, E3a). The modules follow functional schematic blocks (video sync, brick display, ball hit/motion, serve, coin, free game, sound). MAME's driver is also a netlist taken from the same schematic, so the connectivity naturally matches. But the core does not copy MAME's pin-number NET_C organization, its section grouping or its emulator-only shortcuts (the EXTCLOCK clock patterns, the NETDEV_DELAY for C36, the BJT antenna latch model).

findings.signal: one module per TTL chip type, pins as ports
findings.where: rtl/ic/DM9316.sv, SN7474.sv, SN74193.sv, S82S16.sv, DM9312.sv, SN7448.sv, SN74279.sv, DM9602.sv
findings.note: A library of 74xx/93xx part models whose ports use datasheet pin names (CLR_N, LOAD_N, ENP, ENT, RCO, BO_N, CO_N). The board-level modules instantiate them once per physical package.

H/V timing comes from four DM9316 instances L1/K1/M1/N1 with RCO cascade and preset loads (H1c = ~(N4b & VSYNC_N)), plus a 74175 J1 that registers HSYNC/VSYNC/PSYNC/BSYNC. This is the board's counter chain, not a behavioural counter. MAME has the same chips, but as pin-number NET_C lines.

findings.signal: gate-letter net naming from board positions
findings.note: Signals are named by chip and gate section (C2d, H3c, M4b, K4a, F2a, E5b, D5a_Q), a schematic convention. MAME refers to the same nodes only by pin numbers (E3.13, D2.3), so the core's naming is not lifted from the driver text.

findings.signal: brick RAM as an 82S16 chip with the board's address wiring
findings.mame_ref: nl_breakout.cpp: TTL_82S16_DIP(L3) and its NET_C lines
findings.note: The brick memory is one S82S16 instance with H4/H8/H16/V32/V64/V128/V16/RAM_PLAYER1 as address lines and three chip-enable pins driven by decoded raster gates. It is scanned per pixel, as on the board, not stored as a game-state array.

findings.signal: master clock divider modelled from the real F1 9316
findings.mame_ref: nl_breakout.cpp: Clock circuit (#else branch EXTCLOCK Y1/Y2 patterns)
findings.note: CLOCK and CKBH come from a DM9316 F1 and NAND H1d running off the 14.318 MHz source. MAME's default build replaces this with hand-tuned EXTCLOCK duty patterns, and the core does not use those patterns.

findings.mame_ref: nl_breakout.cpp section comments (Hit circuits and start logic, Credit counter logic, Ball logic...)
findings.note: Modules such as ball_hit_motion_controls, ball_serve, empty_wall_detector, numerals_display, score_registers and free_game_selector are wired together through board net names (SERVE_WAIT_N, BTB_HIT_N, CX0/CX1/X2/Y0-Y2). The grouping does not follow MAME's flat netlist sections.

findings.signal: score digits through 9312 muxes and a 7448 decoder
findings.note: Digits go through four DM9312 8:1 muxes, an SN7448 seven-segment decoder and two more 9312s that pick segments from H/V bits. This is how the TTL board draws numerals, with no font ROM or software digit table.

findings.mame_ref: nl_breakout.cpp: Paddles and Playfield logic sections
findings.note: The gate inputs match MAME's NET_C wiring (e.g. E5/E4/D4 paddle counter, A5/A6/B6/C6 ball angle logic). Both come from the same schematic, so a correct core has to share this.

findings.signal: analog parts replaced by FPGA counters
findings.note: The one-shots and the 555 are modelled as clock-count state machines whose COUNTS come from the board's RC values. MAME instead simulates the R/C components. This is ordinary FPGA engineering.

findings.mame_ref: nl_breakout.cpp: Startup / Antenna latch (Q1-Q3 BJTs), C36 NETDEV_DELAY, C9 555 paddle timer
findings.note: The core replaces the BJT start-up latch with a behavioural Q flop, leaves out the C36 brick-gap delay, and takes PAD_OUT from the wrapper instead of a 555 timer. These diverge from MAME's model, but they are abstractions rather than hardware detail.
